attachments.origin_landmark: medial orbital margin, medial palpebral ligament
attachments.insertion_landmark: circumferential around the orbit, lateral palpebral raphe (dermal)

functional_compartments.name: Palpebral part
functional_compartments.innervation_branch: facial n., zygomatic branch, thin fibers
functional_compartments.function_note: Thin fibers within the eyelids themselves; responsible for the involuntary/reflexive blink and for gentle voluntary lid closure (e.g. blinking on command, sleep) -- functionally and architecturally distinct from the orbital part's forceful voluntary closure (adjusted from an earlier draft that described this part as purely involuntary -- caught by adversarial fact-check, see docs/VERIFICATION.md).
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

functional_compartments.name: Orbital part
functional_compartments.function_note: Thicker, more peripheral fibers forming a complete ring around the orbital margin; responsible for the forceful, voluntary 'squeezing shut' closure (e.g. against bright light), unlike the palpebral part's gentle reflexive blink.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: High-frequency linear probe placed perpendicular to a horizontal line drawn laterally from the lateral canthus (the lateral canthus horizontal plane, LCHP), at any of four reference planes used in the source study: through the lateral canthus itself, the orbital rim, the midpoint of the frontal process of the zygomatic bone, or the jugale point. For crow's-feet treatment the classic injection point is 1.5-2.0 cm lateral to the lateral canthus.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: The orbicularis oculi lies superficially, a mean of 4.7-5.5 mm deep to skin (varying by reference plane); the zygomaticus major/minor lie a further 3.0-4.5 mm deeper, immediately beneath the orbicularis oculi's inferior/lateral fibers.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: On Sihler staining, nerve branches converging into the lateral orbicularis oculi were densest in the region corresponding to the 1-4 o'clock arc of a semicircle centered on the orbital rim (using the orbital-rim-to-lateral-margin distance as the radius) -- a reasonable target region for crow's-feet injection. Stereomicroscopy shows the facial nerve travels in the soft tissue beneath the muscle rather than within it, branching superficially to supply the orbital part.
structures_at_risk: zygomaticus major and zygomaticus minor, directly deep to the inferolateral orbicularis oculi -- toxin diffusing past the muscle's own ~4.7-5.5 mm depth can weaken these and impair smiling/upper lip elevation

the anatomically variable lateral muscular band of orbicularis oculi that can extend to the corner of the mouth (mean width ~6.9 mm at the lateral canthus level in one cadaveric series) -- injecting into it can affect mouth-corner movement
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: Because the facial nerve running beneath orbicularis oculi does not terminate discretely within the palpebral vs. orbital parts but courses continuously through the muscle, the authors note that precise anatomical (positional/depth) information is of more practical value than neuromuscular-junction density alone for guiding injection depth and lateral extent.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Piao JZ, Lee JH, Hu KS, Kim HJ, Clin Anat 39(6):662-671 (2025), doi:10.1002/ca.24290 (https://doi.org/10.1002/ca.24290) -- retrieved via PubMed

trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Bridge of the nose and upper lip, sometimes the cheek; described as making 'print jumps' when reading.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Squinting from uncorrected refraction or glare, forward-head reading posture; satellite of sternocleidomastoid (sternal head) trigger points.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons Trigger Point Manual -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded head and neck muscle reference document (Simons DG, Travell JG, Simons LS, Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual, Vol 1, 2nd ed., Williams & Wilkins, 1999; Donnelly JM, Fernandez-de-las-Penas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds), 3rd ed., Wolters Kluwer, 2019)
